title: One 74HC595 drives your 7-segment display with 3 Arduino pins. You want a second digit. How do you add a second 74HC595?
options: Connect Q7' (pin 9) of the first chip to DS (data in) of the second. Share clock and latch.
Connect Q0 of the first chip to the latch pin of the second.
You need 3 new Arduino pins for the second chip.
Connect the two chips with their VCC pins only.
explain: Q7' is the serial output. It passes the bit that falls out of the first register into the second one. Both chips share clock and latch. You send 16 bits with two shiftOut() calls, then one latch pulse. You get 16 outputs for still 3 Arduino pins.

title: Your latch pin stays HIGH all the time, also while shiftOut() runs. What do you see on the display?
options: Nothing changes. The latch pin does not matter.
The segments flicker with half-shifted garbage while the 8 bits move in.
The display stays dark forever.
The chip is damaged.
explain: The shift register and the output register are two stages. Latch LOW to HIGH copies the shift register to the outputs. If the latch is always HIGH (or follows the data), the outputs show every half-shifted state. The right order is: latch LOW, shiftOut(), latch HIGH.

title: A driver shifts the mask, not the bit number. data = 0x96. What does this print?
options: Infinite loop
explain: The mask goes 0x80, 0x40, ... 0x01, then 0, and the loop stops because m is false. No counter can wrap. The first bit printed is bit 7, so this is MSB first, the same order as shiftOut(..., MSBFIRST, ...).

title: A safe way to count 7..0 with an unsigned counter. What does this print?
options: Infinite loop
explain: The test i-- > 0 compares the old value, then decrements. With i = 1 the test is true and i becomes 0, so 0 is printed. With i = 0 the test is false and the loop ends (i wraps to 255, but nobody reads it). This is the safe form of the i >= 0 trap.

title: Simulated 74HC595. You send 0x01 with MSBFIRST. Each clock pushes the register left. What is in the register after 8 clocks?
options: 0xFF
explain: The first bit sent is pushed furthest, so it ends in Q7. The last bit sent (bit 0) ends in Q0. MSBFIRST therefore puts bit 7 of your byte on Q7 and bit 0 on Q0. If your segment wiring is mirrored, switch to LSBFIRST or fix the wires.

title: NPN switches the 24 mA digit current. Pin is 5 V, V_BE = 0.7 V, forced gain 10. Which base resistor in ohms?
explain: I_B = 24 mA / 10 = 2.4 mA. The resistor drops 5 - 0.7 = 4.3 V, so R = 4.3 V / 2.4 mA = 1.79 kOhm. Pick the next lower standard value, 1.8 kOhm or less. Your 1 kOhm gives 4.3 mA: more than needed, still safe for the pin.

title: 4 digits, each lit for 5 ms in turn. How bright is each digit compared to always on, and how often is the whole display refreshed? What does this print?
explain: One full round is 4 x 5 = 20 ms, so the display refreshes at 50 Hz. Each digit is ON for 5 of 20 ms: duty 25%. It looks about a quarter as bright, so multiplexing needs more segment current. Duty is always ON time divided by the whole period, not by the ON time of one digit.

title: The NPN is fully ON (saturated). You change the base resistor from 1.8 kOhm to 1 kOhm. What happens to the segment current?
options: It rises a lot, because I_B is bigger.
It stays almost the same. The segment resistors set it.
It falls, because the base takes more current.
The segments turn off.
explain: A saturated transistor is nearly a closed switch. The collector current is set by the rest of the circuit: supply, LED voltage and the segment resistors. More base current beyond the needed value only wastes a little pin current. Too little base current is the real danger: the transistor leaves saturation and the digit gets dim.

title: Two digits are multiplexed. A faint copy of digit 1 shows on digit 2 (ghosting). Tap the line that causes it.
explain: The digit is switched on before the new segment pattern is latched. For a short time the new digit shows the old pattern. Switch the digit OFF first, shift and latch the new pattern, then switch the digit ON. Here: move the comPin HIGH line after the latch HIGH line.

title: 8 segments x 3 mA = 24 mA would flow out through one Arduino pin (recommended limit 20 mA). You want the same brightness. What is the fix?
options: Add a resistor on the common pin.
Use an NPN on the common pin. The pin only drives the base.
Do nothing. 24 mA is always fine.
Use a bigger Arduino pin number.
explain: A resistor on the common pin only lowers the current, so the segments get dimmer (and it repeats your shared-resistor mistake). A transistor takes the 24 mA itself and the pin gives only a few mA to the base. Pins are for signals. Loads above about 20 mA go through a transistor.
